scenes.text: A closed cylinder contains nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia, already at equilibrium. Nitrogen and hydrogen form ammonia, while ammonia breaks down in the reverse direction. The average opposing rates match. Now imagine pushing the piston down while keeping the temperature constant. Why does this squeeze lead to more ammonia? First separate what the piston does from what the reaction does.

Pushing the piston down reduces the volume. The same gas molecules now occupy less space. Compression itself has not converted nitrogen or hydrogen into ammonia. It has changed the space available to the mixture. Temperature is held constant, so this model does not show the gas being heated or the molecules gaining a higher average speed.

Gas pressure comes from molecules hitting the walls. With less distance to travel, molecules hit the walls more frequently. That raises the pressure before the reaction has changed the mixture. The gauge now shows the higher pressure caused by compression. The cylinder remains closed, so no reacting gas has escaped. Keep that immediate effect separate from the later equilibrium response.

Read the balanced equation. One nitrogen molecule and three hydrogen molecules can form two ammonia molecules. The small g means gas, so all these substances contribute to the amount of gas in the cylinder. Count molecules on each side: four on the left, two on the right. The same nitrogen and hydrogen atoms can therefore be rearranged into fewer gas molecules.

At constant temperature, compression favours the side with fewer gas particles when the gaseous totals differ. In this reaction that means the ammonia side. A net forward reaction produces more ammonia and reduces the total amount of gas. The animation shows the overall rearrangement, not a single four-molecule collision or the detailed reaction pathway. Matter is conserved even though the number of gas molecules changes.

Now hold the piston in its new position and keep the temperature fixed. The pressure rose immediately when the gas was squeezed. As more ammonia forms, fewer gas molecules hit the walls, so pressure falls from that immediate high value. The reaction partly offsets the imposed rise. It does not undo the compression or put the piston back. This graph is a schematic trend, not measured pressure data.

Try the opposite change in the same nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia mixture. Start at equilibrium. Keep the cylinder closed and the temperature constant. Pull the piston up to increase the volume, then hold it there. What happens to pressure immediately? Which reaction direction is favoured afterwards? Explain using the balanced equation. Pause if you need longer.

Pressure falls immediately because the same gas has more space. The reaction then favours the side with more gas particles: nitrogen and hydrogen. Breaking down two ammonia molecules can make one nitrogen and three hydrogen molecules. The increased amount of gas partly offsets the pressure fall. The final pressure need not return to its original value.
